Published in final edited form as: Prog Cardiovasc Dis. 2018 Mar 10;60(6):600–606. doi: 10.1016/j.pcad.2018.03.002 Abstract Peri-procedural management of oral anticoagulants can be complex and confusing for many providers. It involves a careful balance of a patient’s thromboembolic risk and bleeding risk. For every patient chronically taking an oral anticoagulant who will be undergoing an elective procedure, a four step approach may be considered when creating a plan for the oral anticoagulant. (1) Does the oral anticoagulant need to stop for the procedure? (2) If yes, when should the oral anticoagulant be stopped pre-procedure? (3) Does the patient require a “bridging” parenteral anticoagulant? (4) When should anticoagulation be re-started post procedure? Based on the unique features of warfarin versus the direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC), a unique, personalized plan should be developed and tailored to the individual patient. Anticoagulant specialists, such as anticoagulation clinic pharmacists, may help facilitate this process. Keywords: Oral anticoagulant, direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC), warfarin, peri-procedural management Background Each year, an estimated 2 million Americans are diagnosed with either atrial fibrillation (AF) or venous thromboembolism (VTE) and require long-term anticoagulation therapy to prevent serious thromboembolic complications.1 Given an increasing prevalence with age, these patients often require other health care services for prevention or treatment of comorbid conditions. This affects approximately 250,000 patients with atrial fibrillation annually in North America.2 Common procedures for anticoagulated patients include screening endoscopy, cardiac catheterization, urologic surgery, and orthopedic surgery.3 As each of these procedures caries a significant risk of bleeding, it is generally prudent to stop anticoagulants at the time of the surgery. This allows the surgeon to proceed without a significant risk of bleeding. Once operative hemostasis has been achieved, anticoagulation is resumed with an eye towards preventing thromboembolic complications. Traditionally, the only available oral anticoagulant in most of the world was warfarin. Because of a long effective half-life and many drug-drug interactions, a complex peri-procedural management strategy was developed which often involved the use of an overlapping (“bridging”) parenteral anticoagulant while the anticoagulant effect of warfarin wore off pre-procedurally and restarted post-procedurally. This decision-making process involves assessing a patient’s thromboembolic risk as well as the bleeding risk associated with both patient-specific factors and the procedure itself.4 Since 2009, the introduction of four direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) has added additional complexity to this decision-making process. Unlike warfarin, the DOAC medications have a much shorter time-to-onset and half-life, negating the need for any overlapping or “bridging” anticoagulation. A general approach to patients taking chronic oral anticoagulants who are planning to undergo a surgical procedure can be summed up with four important questions: 1. Does the oral anticoagulant need to stop for the procedure? 2. If yes, when should the oral anticoagulant be stopped pre-procedure? 3. Does the patient require a “bridging” parenteral anticoagulant? 4. When should anticoagulation be re-started post-procedure? To answer each of these questions, clinicians must assess the patient’s thromboembolic risk, associated bleeding risks (patient- and procedure-specific), understand the oral anticoagulant’s properties, and assess the patients’ renal function (particularly for patients taking DOAC medications or using “bridging” anticoagulants). Assessing Thromboembolic Risk To best inform the length of time a patient can safely be without systemic anticoagulation, an understanding of thromboembolic risk is paramount. However, little contemporary data is available to guide this process and most risk stratification tools are based largely on expert opinion. For patients with AF, the 2012 American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) guidelines primarily used the Congestive heart failure, Hypertension, Age, Diabetes mellitus, and Stroke (CHADS2) score to classify patients into low, intermediate, and high thromboembolic risk (Table 1).4 A more recent expert consensus document from the American College of Cardiology (ACC) modified these risk elements based on the more recent and commonly used Congestive Heart Failure, Hypertension, Age, Diabetes, Stroke, Vascular Disease, and Sex Category (CHA2DS2-VASc) risk stratification scheme.2 Table 1. The standard bridging protocol for vitamin K antagonist (VKA) patients before surgery is a temporary switch from warfarin to a short-acting anticoagulant, usually to reduce the risk of thromboembolism during the time warfarin is stopped or is wearing off. The core idea is that stopping warfarin leaves the patient vulnerable to clotting, so bridging is intended to fill that gap until surgery is complete and the patient can safely restart anticoagulation afterward [N1-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3].

The temporary anticoagulants most commonly used are low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) and, in some cases, unfractionated heparin. LMWH is preferred in many guidelines and practice materials because it is subcutaneously administered and generally considered more convenient and better tolerated than intravenous unfractionated heparin. The evidence here is explicit: bridging with unfractionated heparin or LMWH aims to reduce thromboembolic risk, and LMWH bridging is specifically described as a standard approach in perioperative management [N1-R2][N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that bridging with LMWH injections should start around 36 hours after the last warfarin dose, usually about 3 days before surgery, and the last dose of LMWH is timed to align with the planned surgery date [N1-R4]. This timing reflects the fact that LMWH has a shorter half-life and can be titrated to the patient’s needs, whereas intravenous heparin is typically used when LMWH is not practical or when more rapid anticoagulation is needed [N2-R3].

As for how long bridging is usually continued before surgery, the evidence points to a typical bridging duration of 10 to 12 days, but that is not universally fixed. The Circulation source explicitly says bridging is usually low-molecular-weight heparin given by subcutaneous injection for 10 to 12 days, which gives a clear standard reference [N3-R2]. However, the evidence also shows that the duration depends on the patient’s thromboembolic risk and the procedure itself. In other words, the bridge is not simply a fixed 10-day period; it is tailored to the individual risk profile and the surgical context [N1-R5][N2-R5]. The bridging regimen is therefore described as “tailored to patients' thromboembolic risk” and “feasible, effective, and safe for many patients” [N2-R5].

In summary, the standard bridging protocol is: stop warfarin, replace it with LMWH or unfractionated heparin during the periprocedural period, and continue bridging long enough to cover the time until surgery and the immediate postoperative phase, typically 10 to 12 days but adjusted by the patient’s risk and surgery type [N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R3][N2-R5][N3-R2].

When bridging is chosen, the decision is shaped by three main factors: patient-specific risk, surgery type and bleeding risk, and institutional protocols, hospital resources, and local guidelines.

First, patient-specific risk is central. The evidence shows that the decision to bridge depends on the patient’s thromboembolic risk, and that risk assessment is a key part of perioperative management. The ACC expert consensus document explicitly says the decision should be guided by the patient’s thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk associated with both patient-specific factors and the procedure itself [N4-F2]. The Uptodate material similarly emphasizes that standardized management protocols have been developed for many patient groups, and that protocols may be modified to allow a patient-centric approach that accounts for individual patient characteristics [N3-F1]. That means higher thromboembolic risk, such as recent venous thromboembolism, recent stroke, or severe thrombophilia, makes bridging more likely [N4-F2]. Conversely, lower thromboembolic risk may make bridging unnecessary or less intense [N3-F1].

Second, surgery type and bleeding risk strongly influence the decision. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that surgery and invasive procedures have associated bleeding risks, and interrupting anticoagulation may transiently increase thromboembolic risk while also increasing bleeding risk [N3-R3][N4-F2]. The UpToDate excerpt notes that if the patient bleeds from the procedure, their anticoagulant may need to be discontinued for a longer period, further increasing thromboembolic risk [N3-F1]. This means the bleeding risk of the specific surgery matters: high-risk procedures may require more aggressive bridging or closer monitoring, while low-risk procedures may allow shorter bridging or even postponement of surgery if possible [N3-R5][N4-F2].

Third, institutional protocols, hospital resources, and local guidelines are important. The evidence shows that bridging is not a one-size-fits-all practice; it depends on institutional protocols and may vary by hospital resources and local guidelines [N1-R1][N3-R3][N3-F1]. The physician’s role in the conversation is already tied to asking whether the patient has discussed protocol specifics with the hospital or local guidelines [N1-R1]. That is because the evidence indicates that bridging can be influenced by what the hospital or local system uses, rather than only by the patient’s individual risk alone [N1-R1][N3-R3].

In short, the choice to bridge is determined by whether the patient’s thromboembolic risk outweighs the bleeding risk of the surgery, and by the hospital’s established protocols and resources [N4-F2][N3-F1][N3-R3]. If the patient has high thromboembolic risk or a procedure with high bleeding risk, bridging is more likely. If the hospital or local guidelines recommend a different approach, that will also shape the protocol [N1-R1][N3-R3].

## Final integrated answer to your question

The short answer is: **you should follow the standard bridging protocol only if your doctor determines it is needed after assessing your thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk of your surgery; otherwise, it may not be needed at all** [N4-F2][N3-F1][N3-R5].

### 1) What bridging means and why it is needed when stopping warfarin

Bridging is a temporary switch from warfarin to a short-acting anticoagulant. The goal is to reduce the risk of thromboembolism during the time warfarin is stopped or is wearing off, because stopping warfarin can leave you vulnerable to blood clots [N1-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3]. In other words, bridging fills the gap between when warfarin is stopped and when it can safely be restarted after surgery [N3-R2].

### 2) Which temporary anticoagulants are typically used and how they differ

The most commonly used temporary anticoagulants are **low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH)** and, in some cases, **unfractionated heparin**. LMWH is generally preferred because it is subcutaneously administered and is often considered more convenient and better tolerated than intravenous unfractionated heparin [N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that bridging with unfractionated heparin or LMWH aims to reduce thromboembolic risk [N1-R2].

### 3) How long bridging is usually continued before surgery

The standard bridging regimen is often described as **low-molecular-weight heparin given by subcutaneous injection for 10 to 12 days** [N3-R2]. However, this is not a universal fixed schedule. The evidence shows that the duration is tailored to the patient’s thromboembolic risk and the procedure itself [N1-R5][N2-R5]. In practice, LMWH bridging may start around **36 hours after the last warfarin dose**, usually **about 3 days before surgery** [N1-R4]. So the bridge is not simply a fixed 10-day period; it is adjusted by your individual risk profile and the surgery date [N1-R4][N2-R3].

### 4) When bridging is chosen, what factors affect the choice

The decision to bridge depends on **three main factors**:

#### a) Patient-specific risk factors
The evidence shows that the decision depends on your thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk associated with both patient-specific factors and the procedure itself [N4-F2]. If your thromboembolic risk is higher, bridging is more likely. The ACC expert consensus document explicitly says that standardized management protocols have been developed for many patient groups, and that protocols may be modified to allow a patient-centric approach [N3-F1]. That means your age, comorbidities, recent history of blood clots, and other risk factors will shape the plan [N3-F1][N4-F2].

#### b) Surgery type and bleeding risk
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that surgery and invasive procedures have associated bleeding risks, and interrupting anticoagulation may transiently increase thromboembolic risk while also increasing bleeding risk [N3-R3][N4-F2]. The Uptodate material explains that if the patient bleeds from the procedure, anticoagulation may need to be discontinued for a longer period, further increasing thromboembolic risk [N3-F1]. So the bleeding risk of your surgery is critical: high-risk procedures may require more aggressive bridging or closer monitoring, while lower-risk procedures may allow shorter bridging or even postponement of surgery if possible [N3-R5][N4-F2].

#### c) Institutional protocols, hospital resources, and local guidelines
The evidence shows that bridging is not a one-size-fits-all practice. It depends on institutional protocols, hospital resources, and local guidelines [N1-R1][N3-R3][N3-F1]. The physician’s role is already tied to asking whether you have discussed protocol specifics with the hospital or local guidelines [N1-R1]. That is because the evidence indicates that bridging can vary by what the hospital or local system uses, rather than only by the patient’s individual risk alone [N1-R1][N3-R3].

### 5) When bridging is not needed and what alternatives may be better

Bridging is **not always needed**, and the evidence supports alternatives that may be better in some cases. The ACC document explicitly says that unless a high bleeding-risk surgery is urgently needed, it is best to **postpone the procedure until thromboembolic risk is attenuated** and to **avoid interrupting OACs whenever possible** [N3-R5]. The StatPearls evidence also says that continuing anticoagulation therapy is safe in some procedures, including dental procedures, and that bridging therapy may not be needed [N5-R1]. This means stopping warfarin can sometimes be avoided altogether if the risk of clotting is not high enough to justify the bleeding risk of stopping the drug [N3-R5][N5-R1].

The evidence also shows that continuing anticoagulation versus stopping it is a central issue. The Uptodate material states that interrupting anticoagulation for a procedure may transiently increase thromboembolism risk, while surgery itself increases bleeding risk [N3-F1]. It also says that standardized management protocols have been developed for many patient groups, and that protocols may be modified to allow a patient-centric approach [N3-F1]. So the evidence-based alternative to bridging is not simply “do nothing,” but to manage the procedure while continuing anticoagulation where possible, especially when the risk of stopping is outweighed by the risk of clotting [N3-F1][N5-R1].

### 6) What the patient should ask next and what the physician should explain

The patient should ask for specific details that will make the bridging plan safe and individualized. The evidence says the most important questions are:

- **What is the patient’s thromboembolic risk?**
- **What is the bleeding risk of the surgery?**
- **When should warfarin be stopped?**
- **Does bridging need to be used?**
- **When should anticoagulation be restarted after surgery?** [N4-F2]

The evidence also says clinicians must assess thromboembolic risk, bleeding risk, the oral anticoagulant’s properties, and renal function, especially for DOACs or bridging anticoagulants [N4-F2]. For the patient, the physician should explain that the decision is not simply about “stopping warfarin and then giving something else,” but about **balancing the risks of clotting and bleeding** [N3-F1][N4-F2].

### 7) How to prepare for surgery if bridging is planned

If bridging is planned, the patient should ask:

- **When the last dose of LMWH is scheduled?**
- **Whether the bridge will be started before the procedure?**
- **Whether any preoperative tests or monitoring are needed?** [N1-R4][N2-R3]

The evidence suggests that LMWH bridging may start around **36 hours after the last warfarin dose**, usually **about 3 days before surgery** [N1-R4]. The patient should also ask **how long the bridge will be continued before surgery**, since the standard regimen is **10 to 12 days** but can vary [N2-R3][N3-R2]. In addition, the patient should ask **what happens if bleeding occurs** and **how the plan changes if the surgery is delayed** [N3-F1][N4-F2].

### 8) How to interpret “no bridging needed” for the patient

If your doctor says “no bridging needed,” that does **not automatically mean** that anticoagulation can be stopped freely. Rather, it means that your thromboembolic risk is **low enough** that continuing anticoagulation may be safer than stopping it, and that stopping may not be necessary at all [N3-R5][N5-R1]. The evidence also says the decision should be guided by thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk of the procedure [N4-F2], so the “no bridging needed” conclusion is conditional on your individual situation [N3-F1].

### Bottom line for you

If your doctor says you need a “ponte” before surgery, the standard protocol is:

- **Stop warfarin**,
- **Replace it with LMWH or unfractionated heparin**,
- **Continue bridging for a period tailored to your risk and the surgery**, usually around **3 days before surgery**, with LMWH often continued for **10 to 12 days** [N1-R4][N2-R3][N3-R2].

But **only if** your doctor determines bridging is needed after assessing your risk and the surgery’s bleeding risk. If your doctor says “no bridging needed,” that means stopping warfarin may be safer than bridging, and continuing anticoagulation may be the better option [N3-R5][N5-R1].

### What you should do next

- **Ask your team to explain your thromboembolic risk and the surgery’s bleeding risk.**
- **Ask when warfarin should be stopped and when bridging should start.**
- **Ask when LMWH or the bridging anticoagulant should end.**
- **Ask what happens if bleeding occurs or if the surgery is delayed.**
- **Ask whether your hospital or local guidelines affect the plan.** [N4-F2][N3-F1][N1-R1]

In short: bridging is a **risk-balancing** decision, not a default plan. Your doctor will decide whether it is needed, how long it should last, and what alternative may be better for you [N4-F2][N3-F1][N3-R5].

## Final integrated answer to your question

The short answer is: **you should follow the standard bridging protocol only if your doctor determines it is needed after assessing your thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk of your surgery; otherwise, it may not be needed at all** [N4-F2][N3-F1][N3-R5].

### 1) What bridging means and why it is needed when stopping warfarin

Bridging is a temporary switch from warfarin to a short-acting anticoagulant. The goal is to reduce the risk of thromboembolism during the time warfarin is stopped or is wearing off, because stopping warfarin can leave you vulnerable to blood clots [N1-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3]. In other words, bridging fills the gap between when warfarin is stopped and when it can safely be restarted after surgery [N3-R2].

### 2) Which temporary anticoagulants are typically used and how they differ

The most commonly used temporary anticoagulants are **low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH)** and, in some cases, **unfractionated heparin**. LMWH is generally preferred because it is subcutaneously administered and is often considered more convenient and better tolerated than intravenous unfractionated heparin [N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that bridging with unfractionated heparin or LMWH aims to reduce thromboembolic risk [N1-R2].

### 3) How long bridging is usually continued before surgery

The standard bridging regimen is often described as **low-molecular-weight heparin given by subcutaneous injection for 10 to 12 days** [N3-R2]. However, this is not a universal fixed schedule. The evidence shows that the duration is tailored to the patient’s thromboembolic risk and the procedure itself [N1-R5][N2-R5]. In practice, LMWH bridging may start around **36 hours after the last warfarin dose**, usually **about 3 days before surgery** [N1-R4]. So the bridge is not simply a fixed 10-day period; it is adjusted by your individual risk profile and the surgery date [N1-R4][N2-R3].

### 4) When bridging is chosen, what factors affect the choice

The decision to bridge depends on **three main factors**:

#### a) Patient-specific risk factors
The evidence shows that the decision depends on your thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk associated with both patient-specific factors and the procedure itself [N4-F2]. If your thromboembolic risk is higher, bridging is more likely. The ACC expert consensus document explicitly says that standardized management protocols have been developed for many patient groups, and that protocols may be modified to allow a patient-centric approach [N3-F1]. That means your age, comorbidities, recent history of blood clots, and other risk factors will shape the plan [N3-F1][N4-F2].

#### b) Surgery type and bleeding risk
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that surgery and invasive procedures have associated bleeding risks, and interrupting anticoagulation may transiently increase thromboembolic risk while also increasing bleeding risk [N3-R3][N4-F2]. The Uptodate material explains that if the patient bleeds from the procedure, anticoagulation may need to be discontinued for a longer period, further increasing thromboembolic risk [N3-F1]. So the bleeding risk of your surgery is critical: high-risk procedures may require more aggressive bridging or closer monitoring, while lower-risk procedures may allow shorter bridging or even postponement of surgery if possible [N3-R5][N4-F2].

#### c) Institutional protocols, hospital resources, and local guidelines
The evidence shows that bridging is not a one-size-fits-all practice. It depends on institutional protocols, hospital resources, and local guidelines [N1-R1][N3-R3][N3-F1]. The physician’s role is already tied to asking whether you have discussed protocol specifics with the hospital or local guidelines [N1-R1]. That is because the evidence indicates that bridging can vary by what the hospital or local system uses, rather than only by the patient’s individual risk alone [N1-R1][N3-R3].

The evidence also shows that continuing anticoagulation versus stopping it is a central issue. The Uptodate material states that interrupting anticoagulation for a procedure may transiently increase thromboembolism risk, while surgery itself increases bleeding risk [N3-F1]. It also says that standardized management protocols have been developed for many patient groups, and that protocols may be modified to allow a patient-centric approach [N3-F1]. So the evidence-based alternative to bridging is not simply “do nothing,” but to manage the procedure while continuing anticoagulation where possible, especially when the risk of stopping is outweighed by the risk of clotting [N3-F1][N5-R1].

### 6) What the patient should ask next and what the physician should explain

The patient should ask for specific details that will make the bridging plan safe and individualized. The evidence says the most important questions are:

- **What is the patient’s thromboembolic risk?**
- **What is the bleeding risk of the surgery?**
- **When should warfarin be stopped?**
- **Does bridging need to be used?**
- **When should anticoagulation be restarted after surgery?** [N4-F2]

If bridging is planned, the patient should ask:

- **When the last dose of LMWH is scheduled?**
- **Whether the bridge will be started before the procedure?**
- **Whether any preoperative tests or monitoring are needed?** [N1-R4][N2-R3]

The patient should also ask **how long the bridge will be continued before surgery**, since the standard regimen is **10 to 12 days** but can vary [N2-R3][N3-R2]. If your doctor says “no bridging needed,” that does **not automatically mean** that anticoagulation can be stopped freely. The evidence also says the decision should be guided by thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk of the procedure [N4-F2], so the “no bridging needed” conclusion is conditional on your individual situation [N3-F1].

If your doctor says you need a “ponte” before surgery, the standard protocol is:

- **Stop warfarin**,
- **Replace it with LMWH or unfractionated heparin**,
- **Continue bridging for a period tailored to your risk and the surgery**, usually around **3 days before surgery**, with LMWH often continued for **10 to 12 days** [N1-R4][N2-R3][N3-R2].

- **Ask your team to explain your thromboembolic risk and the surgery’s bleeding risk.**
- **Ask when warfarin should be stopped and when bridging should start.**
- **Ask when LMWH or the bridging anticoagulant should end.**
- **Ask what happens if bleeding occurs or if the surgery is delayed.**
- **Ask whether your hospital or local guidelines affect the plan.** [N4-F2][N3-F1][N1-R1]

## Final integrated answer to your question

The short answer is: **you should follow the standard bridging protocol only if your doctor determines it is needed after assessing your thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk of your surgery; otherwise, it may not be needed at all** [N4-F2][N3-F1][N3-R5].

### 1) What bridging means and why it is needed when stopping warfarin

Bridging is a temporary switch from warfarin to a short-acting anticoagulant. The goal is to reduce the risk of thromboembolism during the time warfarin is stopped or is wearing off, because stopping warfarin can leave you vulnerable to blood clots [N1-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3]. In other words, bridging fills the gap between when warfarin is stopped and when it can safely be restarted after surgery [N3-R2].

### 2) Which temporary anticoagulants are typically used and how they differ

The most commonly used temporary anticoagulants are **low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH)** and, in some cases, **unfractionated heparin**. LMWH is generally preferred because it is subcutaneously administered and is often considered more convenient and better tolerated than intravenous unfractionated heparin [N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that bridging with unfractionated heparin or LMWH aims to reduce thromboembolic risk [N1-R2].

### 3) How long bridging is usually continued before surgery

The standard bridging regimen is often described as **low-molecular-weight heparin given by subcutaneous injection for 10 to 12 days** [N3-R2]. However, this is not a universal fixed schedule. The evidence shows that the duration is tailored to the patient’s thromboembolic risk and the procedure itself [N1-R5][N2-R5]. In practice, LMWH bridging may start around **36 hours after the last warfarin dose**, usually **about 3 days before surgery** [N1-R4]. So the bridge is not simply a fixed 10-day period; it is adjusted by your individual risk profile and the surgery date [N1-R4][N2-R3].

### 4) When bridging is chosen, what factors affect the choice

The decision to bridge depends on **three main factors**:

#### a) Patient-specific risk factors
The evidence shows that the decision depends on your thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk associated with both patient-specific factors and the procedure itself [N4-F2]. If your thromboembolic risk is higher, bridging is more likely. The ACC expert consensus document explicitly says that standardized management protocols have been developed for many patient groups, and that protocols may be modified to allow a patient-centric approach [N3-F1]. That means your age, comorbidities, recent history of blood clots, and other risk factors will shape the plan [N3-F1][N4-F2].

#### b) Surgery type and bleeding risk
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that surgery and invasive procedures have associated bleeding risks, and interrupting anticoagulation may transiently increase thromboembolic risk while also increasing bleeding risk [N3-R3][N4-F2]. The Uptodate material explains that if the patient bleeds from the procedure, anticoagulation may need to be discontinued for a longer period, further increasing thromboembolic risk [N3-F1]. So the bleeding risk of your surgery is critical: high-risk procedures may require more aggressive bridging or closer monitoring, while lower-risk procedures may allow shorter bridging or even postponement of surgery if possible [N3-R5][N4-F2].

#### c) Institutional protocols, hospital resources, and local guidelines
The evidence shows that bridging is not a one-size-fits-all practice. It depends on institutional protocols, hospital resources, and local guidelines [N1-R1][N3-R3][N3-F1]. The physician’s role is already tied to asking whether you have discussed protocol specifics with the hospital or local guidelines [N1-R1]. That is because the evidence indicates that bridging can vary by what the hospital or local system uses, rather than only by the patient’s individual risk alone [N1-R1][N3-R3].

### 5) When bridging is not needed and what alternatives may be better

Bridging is **not always needed**, and the evidence supports alternatives that may be better in some cases. The ACC document explicitly says that unless a high bleeding-risk surgery is urgently needed, it is best to **postpone the procedure until thromboembolic risk is attenuated** and to **avoid interrupting OACs whenever possible** [N3-R5]. The StatPearls evidence also says that continuing anticoagulation therapy is safe in some procedures, including dental procedures, and that bridging therapy may not be needed [N5-R1]. This means stopping warfarin can sometimes be avoided altogether if the risk of clotting is not high enough to justify the bleeding risk of stopping the drug [N3-R5][N5-R1].

The evidence also shows that continuing anticoagulation versus stopping it is a central issue. The Uptodate material states that interrupting anticoagulation for a procedure may transiently increase thromboembolism risk, while surgery itself increases bleeding risk [N3-F1]. It also says that standardized management protocols have been developed for many patient groups, and that protocols may be modified to allow a patient-centric approach [N3-F1]. So the evidence-based alternative to bridging is not simply “do nothing,” but to manage the procedure while continuing anticoagulation where possible, especially when the risk of stopping is outweighed by the risk of clotting [N3-F1][N5-R1].

### 6) What the patient should ask next and what the physician should explain

The patient should ask for specific details that will make the bridging plan safe and individualized. The evidence says the most important questions are:

- **What is the patient’s thromboembolic risk?**
- **What is the bleeding risk of the surgery?**
- **When should warfarin be stopped?**
- **Does bridging need to be used?**
- **When should anticoagulation be restarted after surgery?** [N4-F2]

For the patient, the physician should explain that the decision is not simply about “stopping warfarin and then giving something else,” but about **balancing the risks of clotting and bleeding** [N3-F1][N4-F2].

If bridging is planned, the patient should ask:

- **When the last dose of LMWH is scheduled?**
- **Whether the bridge will be started before the procedure?**
- **Whether any preoperative tests or monitoring are needed?** [N1-R4][N2-R3]

If your doctor says “no bridging needed,” that does **not automatically mean** that anticoagulation can be stopped freely. Rather, it means that your thromboembolic risk is **low enough** that continuing anticoagulation may be safer than stopping it, and that stopping may not be necessary at all [N3-R5][N5-R1]. The evidence also says the decision should be guided by thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk of the procedure [N4-F2], so the “no bridging needed” conclusion is conditional on your individual situation [N3-F1].

### Bottom line for you

If your doctor says you need a “ponte” before surgery, the standard protocol is:

- **Stop warfarin**,
- **Replace it with LMWH or unfractionated heparin**,
- **Continue bridging for a period tailored to your risk and the surgery**, usually around **3 days before surgery**, with LMWH often continued for **10 to 12 days** [N1-R4][N2-R3][N3-R2].

But **only if** your doctor determines bridging is needed after assessing your risk and the surgery’s bleeding risk. If your doctor says “no bridging needed,” that means stopping warfarin may be safer than bridging, and continuing anticoagulation may be the better option [N3-R5][N5-R1].

### What you should do next

- **Ask your team to explain your thromboembolic risk and the surgery’s bleeding risk.**
- **Ask when warfarin should be stopped and when bridging should start.**
- **Ask when LMWH or the bridging anticoagulant should end.**
- **Ask what happens if bleeding occurs or if the surgery is delayed.**
- **Ask whether your hospital or local guidelines affect the plan.** [N4-F2][N3-F1][N1-R1]

In short: bridging is a **risk-balancing** decision, not a default plan. Your doctor will decide whether it is needed, how long it should last, and what alternative may be better for you [N4-F2][N3-F1][N3-R5].

## Final integrated answer to your question

The short answer is: **you should follow the standard bridging protocol only if your doctor determines it is needed after assessing your thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk of your surgery; otherwise, it may not be needed at all** [N4-F2][N3-F1][N3-R5].

### 1) What bridging means and why it is needed when stopping warfarin

Bridging is a temporary switch from warfarin to a short-acting anticoagulant. The goal is to reduce the risk of thromboembolism during the time warfarin is stopped or is wearing off, because stopping warfarin can leave you vulnerable to blood clots [N1-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3]. In other words, bridging fills the gap between when warfarin is stopped and when it can safely be restarted after surgery [N3-R2].

### 2) Which temporary anticoagulants are typically used and how they differ

The most commonly used temporary anticoagulants are **low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH)** and, in some cases, **unfractionated heparin**. LMWH is generally preferred because it is subcutaneously administered and is often considered more convenient and better tolerated than intravenous unfractionated heparin [N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that bridging with unfractionated heparin or LMWH aims to reduce thromboembolic risk [N1-R2].

### 3) How long bridging is usually continued before surgery

The standard bridging regimen is often described as **low-molecular-weight heparin given by subcutaneous injection for 10 to 12 days** [N3-R2]. However, this is not a universal fixed schedule. The evidence shows that the duration is tailored to the patient’s thromboembolic risk and the procedure itself [N1-R5][N2-R5]. In practice, LMWH bridging may start around **36 hours after the last warfarin dose**, usually **about 3 days before surgery** [N1-R4]. So the bridge is not simply a fixed 10-day period; it is adjusted by your individual risk profile and the surgery date [N1-R4][N2-R3].

### 4) When bridging is chosen, what factors affect the choice

The decision to bridge depends on **three main factors**:

#### a) Patient-specific risk factors
The evidence shows that the decision depends on your thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk associated with both patient-specific factors and the procedure itself [N4-F2]. If your thromboembolic risk is higher, bridging is more likely. The ACC expert consensus document explicitly says that standardized management protocols have been developed for many patient groups, and that protocols may be modified to allow a patient-centric approach [N3-F1]. That means your age, comorbidities, recent history of blood clots, and other risk factors will shape the plan [N3-F1][N4-F2].

#### b) Surgery type and bleeding risk
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that surgery and invasive procedures have associated bleeding risks, and interrupting anticoagulation may transiently increase thromboembolic risk while also increasing bleeding risk [N3-R3][N4-F2]. The Uptodate material explains that if the patient bleeds from the procedure, anticoagulation may need to be discontinued for a longer period, further increasing thromboembolic risk [N3-F1]. So the bleeding risk of your surgery is critical: high-risk procedures may require more aggressive bridging or closer monitoring, while lower-risk procedures may allow shorter bridging or even postponement of surgery if possible [N3-R5][N4-F2].

#### c) Institutional protocols, hospital resources, and local guidelines
The evidence shows that bridging is not a one-size-fits-all practice. It depends on institutional protocols, hospital resources, and local guidelines [N1-R1][N3-R3][N3-F1]. The physician’s role is already tied to asking whether you have discussed protocol specifics with the hospital or local guidelines [N1-R1]. That is because the evidence indicates that bridging can vary by what the hospital or local system uses, rather than only by the patient’s individual risk alone [N1-R1][N3-R3].

### 5) When bridging is not needed and what alternatives may be better

Bridging is **not always needed**, and the evidence supports alternatives that may be better in some cases. The ACC document explicitly says that unless a high bleeding-risk surgery is urgently needed, it is best to **postpone the procedure until thromboembolic risk is attenuated** and to **avoid interrupting OACs whenever possible** [N3-R5]. The StatPearls evidence also says that continuing anticoagulation therapy is safe in some procedures, including dental procedures, and that bridging therapy may not be needed [N5-R1]. This means stopping warfarin can sometimes be avoided altogether if the risk of clotting is not high enough to justify the bleeding risk of stopping the drug [N3-R5][N5-R1].

The evidence also shows that continuing anticoagulation versus stopping it is a central issue. The Uptodate material states that interrupting anticoagulation for a procedure may transiently increase thromboembolism risk, while surgery itself increases bleeding risk [N3-F1]. It also says that standardized management protocols have been developed for many patient groups, and that protocols may be modified to allow a patient-centric approach [N3-F1]. So the evidence-based alternative to bridging is not simply “do nothing,” but to manage the procedure while continuing anticoagulation where possible, especially when the risk of stopping is outweighed by the risk of clotting [N3-F1][N5-R1].

### 6) What the patient should ask next and what the physician should explain

The patient should ask for specific details that will make the bridging plan safe and individualized. The evidence says the most important questions are:

- **What is the patient’s thromboembolic risk?**
- **What is the bleeding risk of the surgery?**
- **When should warfarin be stopped?**
- **Does bridging need to be used?**
- **When should anticoagulation be restarted after surgery?** [N4-F2]

The evidence also says clinicians must assess thromboembolic risk, bleeding risk, the oral anticoagulant’s properties, and renal function, especially for DOACs or bridging anticoagulants [N4-F2]. For the patient, the physician should explain that the decision is not simply about “stopping warfarin and then giving something else,” but about **balancing the risks of clotting and bleeding** [N3-F1][N4-F2].

### 7) How to prepare for surgery if bridging is planned

If bridging is planned, the patient should ask:

- **When the last dose of LMWH is scheduled?**
- **Whether the bridge will be started before the procedure?**
- **Whether any preoperative tests or monitoring are needed?** [N1-R4][N2-R3]

The evidence suggests that LMWH bridging may start around **36 hours after the last warfarin dose**, usually **about 3 days before surgery** [N1-R4]. The patient should also ask **how long the bridge will be continued before surgery**, since the standard regimen is **10 to 12 days** but can vary [N2-R3][N3-R2]. In addition, the patient should ask **what happens if bleeding occurs** and **how the plan changes if the surgery is delayed** [N3-F1][N4-F2].

### 8) How to interpret “no bridging needed” for the patient

If your doctor says “no bridging needed,” that does **not automatically mean** that anticoagulation can be stopped freely. Rather, it means that your thromboembolic risk is **low enough** that continuing anticoagulation may be safer than stopping it, and that stopping may not be necessary at all [N3-R5][N5-R1]. The evidence also says the decision should be guided by thromboembolic risk and the bleeding risk of the procedure [N4-F2], so the “no bridging needed” conclusion is conditional on your individual situation [N3-F1].

### Bottom line for you

If your doctor says you need a “ponte” before surgery, the standard protocol is:

- **Stop warfarin**,
- **Replace it with LMWH or unfractionated heparin**,
- **Continue bridging for a period tailored to your risk and the surgery**, usually around **3 days before surgery**, with LMWH often continued for **10 to 12 days** [N1-R4][N2-R3][N3-R2].

But **only if** your doctor determines bridging is needed after assessing your risk and the surgery’s bleeding risk. If your doctor says “no bridging needed,” that means stopping warfarin may be safer than bridging, and continuing anticoagulation may be the better option [N3-R5][N5-R1].

### What you should do next

- **Ask your team to explain your thromboembolic risk and the surgery’s bleeding risk.**
- **Ask when warfarin should be stopped and when bridging should start.**
- **Ask when LMWH or the bridging anticoagulant should end.**
- **Ask what happens if bleeding occurs or if the surgery is delayed.**
- **Ask whether your hospital or local guidelines affect the plan.** [N4-F2][N3-F1][N1-R1]

In short: bridging is a **risk-balancing** decision, not a default plan. Your doctor will decide whether it is needed, how long it should last, and what alternative may be better for you [N4-F2][N3-F1][N3-R5].
